source.title: Revisiting Random Weight Perturbation for Efficiently Improving Generalization
source.authors: Tao Li; Qing-Hua Tao; Wei-Hao Yan; Ying-Wen Wu; Zehao Lei; Kun Fang; Mingzhen He; Xiao-Lin Huang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some figure text is garbled, but the tables and result descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out classification accuracy under random weight perturbation and compares it with SGD and SAM. This is a different intervention aimed at generalization than the claim versions’ listed tests.
record.gate_note: The paper tests random weight perturbation methods on natural-label image classification and reports final test accuracy. Its CIFAR and ImageNet results do not test fitting random labels, width past interpolation, convolution versus fully connected architectures, adaptive optimizers’ generalization under tuning, batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Training-loss and loss-landscape figures are not included as rows because they do not directly report the claim’s train-test gap measure.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flat-minima/generalization connection to develop perturbation-based training methods and compares their performance. It does not test any specified version. In particular, filter-normalized landscape plots and Hessian spectra do not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure against generalization gaps among similarly fitted networks.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that mixing the original loss with the perturbed objective improves the convergence/generalization trade-off, while historical-gradient-guided perturbations further improve performance. Their efficiency claim distinguishes computation from elapsed time: mixed methods require twice SGD's computation, with time savings relying on parallel gradient calculations.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains with random or adversarial weight perturbations, compares these methods on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, and reports test accuracy rather than the target claim’s train-test gap or random-label memorization outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: Using the same versus different data batches changes SAM’s CIFAR-100 ResNet-18 accuracy; m-ARWP results are comparable across those batch choices. Perturbation variance and method settings are swept, with performance differences described in the text and figures.

fits_no_version.finding: Improved random perturbation methods raise held-out accuracy in many settings. For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-100, m-ARWP reaches 81.38±0.12 versus SGD's 78.10±0.39 and SAM's 80.48±0.25. Plain RWP sometimes matches or falls below the baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixed and adaptive random weight perturbations can improve image-classification accuracy, with gains depending on model, dataset, and perturbation method.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 6.2 reports that RWP and ARWP appear flatter in filter-normalized landscape plots than SAM and m-ARWP despite worse generalization and larger dominant Hessian eigenvalues. Training convergence also differs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Visual landscape flatness can disagree with Hessian-based flatness and held-out performance across perturbation-training methods.

record.problems: The experiments report test accuracy but do not provide paired training errors, so train-test gaps cannot be computed from the reported tables. The described plots do not give precise extractable values in the supplied text. ImageNet table results do not report uncertainty; CIFAR table values use three trials.
record.rows_left_out: More than 60 separate model-method-dataset accuracy cells are reported. Retained the complete CIFAR-10/100 rows for VGG16-BN, ResNet-18, WRN-28-10 and ViT-S, then the ImageNet rows through ResNet-18 in Table 3, stopping at the 60-row cap; omitted ImageNet ResNet-50 and ViT-S/32 table results.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe; chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Width sweeps beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks, local connectivity, and initialization transfer.
Matched adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons and effects of tuning, weight decay, or optimizer switching.
Large-batch penalties under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove them. Using different batches for two gradient calculations does not isolate this comparison.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus train-test gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Identification and removal of highly memorized examples, retraining, and comparison with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: All row-version links remain none; these accuracy cells are method evaluations rather than evidence for V1–V8. The record's broader suggestion that the paper lacks train-test-gap measurements needs correction: Figure 3(a) explicitly reports generalization gaps alongside training losses across perturbation settings, although precise values are unavailable in the supplied text. That figure still does not measure V7's sharpness-gap relationship. Figure 5 likewise does not establish a challenge to V7 because its measures and convergence conditions differ. No omitted result tests a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural versus random labels are not tested.
No width sweep past the zero-training-error threshold is reported.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison is reported.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD under limited tuning is reported.
No batch-size comparison or fixed-epoch large-batch penalty is tested.
Dropout is not ablated as an intervention; a ViT dropout rate is only specified in setup.
The study visualizes loss landscapes and Hessian spectra but does not test magnitude-aware sharpness against train-test gaps.
No memorized-example identification, removal, or retraining experiment is reported.
